arbh.front: In the ḥadīth “I have been commanded to fight the people”, which phrase is the evidence for the Sharīʿah's criminal law?
Why does a society need criminal law, according to the notes on Arbaʿīn 8?
arbh.back: It needs a working system of governance to regulate behaviour — and criminal law is one aspect of the Sharīʿah

arbh.front: Besides punishment, what does the Sharīʿah's criminal law focus on?
What two purposes do the Sharīʿah's punishments serve?
arbh.back: They deter people from committing crimes, and they expiate the crime for those who committed it

arbh.front: How does the Sharīʿah differ from every other system of law, according to the notes on Arbaʿīn 8?
arbh.back: It is first and foremost divine, revealed by the Creator of the heavens, the earth and humans; every other system is man-made. And it is suitable for all times and places.

arbh.front: What certainty must Muslims have about the Sharīʿah, and what should they want for others?
arbh.back: Absolute certainty in its justice and morality — and they should want others to have it too, with naṣīḥah: sincerely intending good for them

arbh.front: If the Sharīʿah is divine, how can its application be flawed?
arbh.back: Because the humans applying it are flawed

arbh.text: How to approach a ḥadīth, in order: {{c1::check its authenticity — <bdi>صَحِيح</bdi> or <bdi>حَسَن</bdi>, <bdi>لِذَاتِهِ</bdi> or <bdi>لِغَيْرِهِ</bdi>}}; {{c2::understand it, with its versions}}; {{c3::gather all the aḥādīth on the topic and the relevant verses of the Qurʾān}}; {{c4::see how the Companions and the salaf understood it}}; {{c5::look at the scholarly consensus}}; and only then reach a conclusion
arbh.extra: Taken alone, in a vacuum, a ḥadīth like Arbaʿīn 8 leads to a badly flawed conclusion.
